source.title_on_document: How Students Develop Creative Skills and Critical Thinking with ChatGPT: Experimental Results

paper_design_summary: Over ten weeks (February to May 2024), undergraduate international-relations students at Moscow State University did weekly homework either with AI chatbots only or with any resource except chatbots. The authors scored an entrance essay and a final conference-abstract text (both written in class in two academic hours without auxiliary materials) for four critical-thinking parameters and eight Guilford creativity parameters, using initial scores of 0, 0.5, or 1 point, with 0.5 or 1 point added for improvement (PDF p. 5, journal p. 642, Section 2; Tables 1-2, PDF pp. 7-8, journal pp. 644-645). Only the 16 students who consented to publication are reported, 8 per group, with per-student start and final scores and no statistical tests.

studies.label: Ten-week course experiment (AI chatbots only vs traditional sources)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Homework resource for the semester: AI-powered chatbots only versus any traditional source except chatbots
assignment.quote: Students independently chose a way to accomplish a task during semester. ... Once a method of completing an assignment (“AI” or “traditional”) was selected during the semester, that method could not be changed.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (journal p. 640), Section 2 Materials and methods

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Homework prepared using only AI-powered chatbots (any publicly available chatbots, several allowed)

arms.name: Other sources
arms.description: Homework prepared with any traditional source (books, online resources, classmates, social media, search engines, dictionaries) except chatbots

participants.exclusions: All second- and third-year students took part, but only 16 consented to publication of their results; the total number of participants is not given. Students who missed a task were excluded from the experiment (number not stated).
participants.who: Second- and third-year undergraduate international-relations students, course taught in English
participants.quote: Sixteen people participated in the study. Eight people used AI; eight people used any other resources for homework.
participants.locator: p. 644, Section 4 Results; also p. 640 (only 16 students gave consent) and Tables 1-2 (N = 16)

ai_tool.name_model: Any publicly available AI chatbots (ChatGPT named in title); no predetermined model
ai_tool.how_used: Used as the only information source for weekly homework essays and reports, without instructor feedback; not available for the scored entrance and final in-class texts

task.description: Weekly essays and reports on international-relations topics; scored outputs were an entrance essay and a final text in conference-abstract format (max 500 words) on actuality, problem, research question, and solution method
task.duration: Ten weeks; entrance and final texts two academic hours each

eligibility.reason: Students independently chose their method rather than receiving random assignment (PDF p. 3, journal p. 640, Section 2). Only 16 students are analyzed, 8 AI and 8 other sources (PDF p. 7, journal p. 644, Section 4 and Tables 1-2), below the 50-person core threshold. Creativity is scored on written outputs produced without auxiliary materials (PDF p. 4, journal p. 641, Section 2; PDF pp. 7-8, journal pp. 644-645, Tables 1-2). This non-randomized comparison is observational context under codebook Section 3 and the form-spec quasi_people field note; codebook Section 13 flags that context policy for Review 1.

one_line_finding: With 16 students (8 per group), the authors report no tests but say original thinking improved more in the no-chatbot group (Table 1, p. 644) while creativity parameters such as fluency showed more progress in the chatbot group (Table 2 and text, p. 645).
notes: The abstract and body conflict on creative skills: the Abstract says "The results showed that critical thinking parameters and creative skills have been comparatively underdeveloped in the experimental group." (PDF p. 1, journal p. 638), whereas the Results say "In general, more progress can be seen in the students who used AI." and the Conclusion lists fluency, elaboration, tolerance of ambiguity, breadth of interest, sensitivity, and reflection as parameters in which AI users progressed (PDF p. 8, journal p. 645, Sections 4-5). The one-line finding follows the body; the contrary abstract claim is unresolved. The authors explicitly report no statistical analysis (PDF p. 6, journal p. 643, Section 3); their words significant and insignificant describe score changes, not statistical tests. Direction codes summarize their descriptive statements, and no group means, effect sizes, or tests have been calculated. Start/final pairs retain the printed student order: AI Students 1-8 and Other sources Students 9-16; decimal commas are rendered as decimal points (PDF pp. 7-8, journal pp. 644-645, Tables 1-2).
